newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Ties between Cambodian parties sink to new low.
newsitem.headline: Ties between Cambodian parties sink to new low.

text.p: Relations between Cambodia's two leading political parties have plumbed new depths, raising fears about the future of their coalition government more than one year before general elections are due.

"Relations have reached an all-time low," said one Western analyst of the ill-feeling between the royalist FUNCINPEC party of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP).

The tensions have left an undercurrent of fear and uncertainty in the capital, with many Cambodian families opting to spend their time at home during the April 13-16 Cambodian New Year holiday rather than touring the city and attending fairs.
"If the army do not get involved it's OK, I think we can settle it peacefully," Information Secretary of State and CPP member of parliament Khieu Kanharith said on Thursday.
"I hope the two parties are wise enough not to ask for military backup," he added.
He was speaking a day after the national police chief and the armed forces chief of staff, both members of the CPP, ordered police to step up security and told soldiers to remain in their barracks.
The former battlefield foes have always between suspicious of one another since forming an uneasy but workable coalition after U.N.-run polls in 1993, which followed years of war.

Relations soured in March 1996, when Ranariddh earned the wrath of Hun Sen by threatening to pull out of the government if FUNCINPEC was not given more power to reflect its narrow win over the CPP in the 1993 elections.
The two sides briefly worked together again to win over thousands of Khmer Rouge guerrillas who defected after former rebel official Ieng Sary split with hardliners last August.
A European analyst said the coalition had, in effect, ceased to exist.
He and others said relations had worsened dramatically since a March 30 grenade attack on a demonstration led by opposition leader Sam Rainsy, a FUNCINPEC ally.

They cited as another flash-point the failed bid by former FUNCINPEC secretary general Prince Norodom Sirivudh to return home from exile this week to fight his 1996 conviction on charges linked to an alleged plot to kill Hun Sen.
Airlines have refused to fly Sirivudh to Cambodia after Phnom Penh said he would be would be arrested on arrival.
A further cause for tension has been a split in the royalist ranks led by a former CPP member, Minister of State Ung Phan, who has criticised Ranariddh's leadership.

"There is a serious risk of confrontation and it will depend on the ability of the moderates (in both parties)...to oppose any attempt by the the others to use force to solve their dispute," said the European Cambodia-watcher.
"It would be in the interest of none of the two parties to provoke an armed confrontation," he added.
The streets of the capital appeared calm on Thursday with no unusually heavy security visible, although the two premiers have taken to travelling with large security backup.
The feuding has been a dampener on foreign investment interest in Cambodia, just a few months before the country hopes to join the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN), businessmen said.
"I think it's only likely to affect new investors who are looking at Cambodia from outside," said a British businessman, adding: "I think it has affected tourists."
FUNCINPEC memmber of parliament Ahmad Yahya, acknowledging that ties between the two parties were at a "very, very low level", believed the coalition could survive.
"I don't think the coalition will break up, but it will be bad like this until the elections," he told Reuters, referring to general elections expected in November 1998.
One analyst said he was not so sure elections would take place. "No one knows what will happen in six months," he said.
